Eclipse Planner · LCO network · 40 cm telescopes

What to image now

One click returns the best eclipsing binaries from this moment on, and for each star you pick — a list of time windows ready to enter by hand in LCO. Every window is checked to be fully observable, padding included, from a site that has a 40 cm telescope.

Network sites with a 40 cm telescope

Wise Observatory is not on the list — it has a 1 m telescope only. Ali Observatory is still being built and has no active telescopes.

Parameters

The search starts from the moment you click. Magnitude 13 is a deliberate default — on a 40 cm telescope a star fainter than 13 gives too low a signal-to-noise ratio for eclipse photometry.

The windows in the table go into the request as they are. You set the exposure time — the number of exposures, the block length, the cadence and the baseline all follow from it and from the window length. A primary and a secondary eclipse download as two separate requests, because a request is carried out in only one of its windows.
Only v and rp have actually been verified against the portal. Proper motion and parallax are not in the catalogue — for a high proper-motion star take them from SIMBAD and fill them in here, otherwise leave them at zero.
The epoch trap. As long as the proper motion is zero, the epoch field changes nothing. The moment you fill it in, LCO rolls the position forward from the epoch you declared — so it has to match the coordinates. The coordinates here come from Gaia and are not necessarily J2000. If you take a proper motion from SIMBAD, take the coordinates and their epoch from there too.
Data sources. Ephemerides, eclipse duration and depth for short-period systems from Gaia DR3 (the vari_eclipsing_binary table), which carries an explicit frequency error from which the uncertainty is computed. Detached systems with a sharp eclipse from GCVS 5.1, whose periods rest on a long time baseline and are therefore more accurate than Gaia for narrow eclipses. Names and variable classifications from AAVSO VSX.

Updated ephemerides from VarAstro. For stars marked VarAstro in the uncertainty column, the period and the time of minimum were taken from an export of VarAstro, maintained from a database of hundreds of thousands of observed minima. These are the freshest data available, and they include the actually measured phase of the secondary minimum instead of assuming it is 0.5. VarAstro does not publish a period error, so their uncertainty is computed from a conservative assumption of 10⁻⁵ of the period — about a minute and a half after three months, about five minutes after a year. Because the reference epoch is recent, the near-term drift is negligible.

The timing uncertainty is also given as a number for stars whose ephemeris comes from Gaia, where the frequency error was measured and published. It is recomputed for every date, as the period error times the number of cycles elapsed since the reference epoch, and so grows the further you get from it. It does not include real period changes — mass transfer, or a light-time effect from a third companion.

What is not included. Stars whose only ephemeris comes from GCVS were removed from the database entirely. No period error is published there, and calibrating against Gaia showed the real error to be 6.8 times the published precision at the median and 120 times at the 90th percentile — meaning any number shown for them would have been fiction. An example: FP Sge, whose epoch is from 1934; after 52,524 cycles the deviation reaches two hours. Every row in the table rests on an ephemeris whose error can be quantified.

To verify. Cross-reference against VarAstro's minima predictions — the link on each star's name searches for it there directly. The tool does not account for cloud, a local horizon, or the Moon.

How the windows are chosen. Each window runs from the eclipse start minus the padding to the eclipse end plus the padding. The tool checks that the whole window — not just the eclipse — falls inside the site's dark window and stays above the altitude threshold from start to finish. A window where only the eclipse itself qualifies is not included, because the scheduler would not be able to carry it out. The number of sites on each row is a measure of the chance the request gets scheduled: a window caught from three sites competes for three systems in parallel.
